analysis.one_liner: Has patent examiners and FDA share drug-approval information to weed out weak drug patents.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate committee approved the bill with amendments in April 2025, and it now sits on the Senate calendar with no floor vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill creates a standing task force so the Patent Office and the FDA share information about drug and biologic patents and approvals. Patent examiners would learn when a drug approval or labeling change happens, and could see FDA application information that is not public, so they can better judge whether a drug patent deserves to be granted. The goal is fewer patents granted on drugs that don't deserve them, which is one reason generic and cheaper versions of drugs get delayed.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers benefit indirectly, when fewer weak drug patents are granted and cheaper generic and biosimilar versions can reach the market sooner. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers benefit because they face fewer marginal patents to challenge in court, which is expensive and slow. The Patent Office also gains, since examiners get better information to make accurate decisions.

how_it_helps.text: The bill establishes an Interagency Task Force on Patents requiring the Patent Office and FDA to share information on how each evaluates applications and on new approvals of patents, drugs, and biologics [S2] [S3].

It creates a process requiring the Patent Office to request FDA information relevant to patent applications, including non-public communications between FDA and drug sponsors, so examiners can check things like whether an invention was on sale before the filing date [S3].

The bill directs the Patent Office to assist FDA in its ministerial role of listing patents, and requires the USPTO Director to report to Congress within four years on how often FDA information is used in patent examinations [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies bear the main cost: patents that would previously have been granted may now face tougher examination because examiners will see FDA data that was previously out of their view. Drug sponsors also get new obligations — they must be given 30 days' notice before their confidential FDA information is shared with the Patent Office, and both agencies must build confidentiality protocols. The administrative cost of running the task force falls on the two agencies.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives drug sponsors a 30-day window to consult before their confidential FDA information is shared with patent examiners, and lets the agencies share confidential records between themselves — a real, if safeguarded, leakage risk that the bill itself requires protocols and remedies for [S3].

It is an information-coordination measure, not a fix for the main drug-patent problems: it does not change how many patents can be listed in FDA's Orange Book, does not limit patent thickets, and does not affect patent term or litigation. Its effect on drug prices will be indirect and slow.

Better sharing of confidential FDA data with the Patent Office could arguably make examination harder for genuinely novel drugs too, adding uncertainty for all pharmaceutical patents, not just weak ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a modest, low-cost administrative reform with a plausible but indirect benefit for patients: better patent examination quality, which over time means fewer weak drug patents standing between people and cheaper generics. The drawbacks — confidentiality risk in sharing FDA data and the 30-day sponsor consultation — are addressed with protocols but cannot be eliminated. The honest limitation is scope: this bill works at the Patent Office stage and does nothing about the volume of patents listed with FDA or the litigation tactics that most often delay generics, so it should be judged as a piece of the puzzle, not a drug-price fix.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it with amendments and put it on the Senate's calendar of business in April 2025, but no floor vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 24, 2025 by Senator Durbin with Senators Tillis, Grassley, Coons, and Welch, and was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee [S3] [S5].
On April 3, 2025 the Judiciary Committee ordered the bill reported with amendments favorably, and on April 10 it was reported by Senator Grassley with amendments [S5].
On April 10, 2025 the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 41, where it awaits a floor vote that has not been scheduled [S3] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet — the bill passed committee with bipartisan support but is waiting on the Senate calendar for a floor vote that has not been scheduled. Until that happens, the existing information gap between the Patent Office and FDA continues, which is most useful to brand-name drug makers whose marginal patents face no extra scrutiny.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Still open — awaiting a Senate floor vote

sides.party_line_note: The bill's original cosponsors were three Democrats (Durbin, Coons, Welch) and two Republicans (Tillis, Grassley), and it cleared the Judiciary Committee with amendments in April 2025 [S3] [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Patent examiners will be able to see FDA approval data and non-public sponsor communications, making it harder to obtain marginal drug patents and easier for examiners to spot claims that lack novelty. Weaker patents are the main tool that delays generic and biosimilar competition, which costs patients money.
Better patent examination means fewer dubious patents to work around or challenge in court, a process generic makers often cannot afford. That should mean earlier entry and lower drug prices.
Both agencies take on the work of running a task force, building confidentiality protocols, and processing information-sharing requests, in exchange for better decision-making data on both sides.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has bipartisan sponsorship and a favorable committee report and now sits on the Senate calendar. Bills at this stage often wait a long time unless the Majority Leader schedules a floor vote; with five bipartisan cosponsors it could plausibly pass by unanimous consent, but it would then need companion action in the House to become law.
